title: Laughter (Genesis 21:1–7)
hookLine: Sarah laughs at ninety and names her son Isaac, he laughs

lines: WHITE HAIR IN THE MATERNITY WARD.
cards: A maternity ward. A woman in the bed with white hair. A husband in the chair beside her, a hundred years old, holding a newborn.
A nurse walks in, stops, and checks the chart twice. That's the scene in Genesis twenty-one, and the Bible knows exactly how funny it is.

Long after the call to go forth, after the stars and the visitors at the tent, the promise finally arrives. And the whole story of it, from the first announcement to the birth, is threaded with one sound. Not weeping.

teach.b: First, the laughs before. When God first tells Abraham, in chapter seventeen, that Sarah will bear a son, Abraham falls on his face and laughs. A hundred years old, and Sarah ninety?
Then at Mamre, when the visitor promises a son by next year, Sarah, listening behind the tent door, laughs to herself. Old and worn out, she thinks, and pleasure now?
The visitor asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is there any thing hard to God?" Sarah, embarrassed, says she didn't laugh. And he says: yes, you did.
Second, the birth. The Lord visits Sarah as he promised, and she bears a son in her old age, at the very time God said. Third, the name.

In Hebrew, Yitzchak: he laughs. The doubting laugh is turned into a name. And Sarah, holding the baby, says, in the Douay-Rheims: "God hath made a laughter for me: whosoever shall hear of it will laugh with me."
The laugh has changed. It started as a snort at the impossible. It ends as joy so big she expects the neighbors to catch it.
Fourth, the echo. The visitor's question comes back in the Gospel of Luke.
When the angel Gabriel tells Mary she'll bear a son, he points to her elderly cousin Elizabeth, pregnant at last, and says that nothing is impossible with God.

teach.h: GOD HATH MADE A LAUGHTER FOR ME.
teach.b: Old Sarah and young Mary, two births that make no sense, and the same question underneath: is anything too hard for God?

how: Catholics remember Sarah and Abraham as parents in faith, and the Church reads the promise of Isaac alongside the announcement to Mary, where the angel says nothing is impossible with God.

o: a scornful sound that God punishes in Sarah
doubt turned to joy at Isaac's birth
the mocking of neighbors at an old couple

games.q: what's inside the laughter — tap the pairs.

s: only Sarah laughs at God's promise
Abraham laughs first, falling on his face, in chapter seventeen.
Yitzchak: the doubting laugh becomes a name.
Sarah admits right away that she laughed
she says she didn't, and the visitor says yes, you did.

games.q: you're Sarah, ninety, holding a newborn son. a year ago you laughed at the idea behind a tent door. what do you say now?
o: I always knew it would happen.
God hath made a laughter for me, and everyone who hears will laugh with me.
games.why: "God hath made a laughter for me: whosoever shall hear of it will laugh with me." the snort of doubt has become joy she expects to share.

practice: Look back over your life for something you were sure would never happen, and then did: a friendship out of nowhere, a recovery nobody expected, a second chance. Let yourself smile at it, and if a real laugh comes, let it.
If you pray, give thanks for the surprise that still makes you laugh.

wordCard.voice: Laughter. The sound that runs through the birth of Isaac, whose name means he laughs. It starts as doubt and ends as joy.

orig.note: Hebrew: Isaac, he laughs. the name keeps the joke of his birth.

carryVoice: Your line: god made me laugh. Old Sarah got the last laugh after all. Day three hundred fifty-one, in the books.
